newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU moves to help calves inadequate, activists say.
newsitem.headline: EU moves to help calves inadequate, activists say.

text.p: Animal rights groups said on Wednesday new European Union measures to improve the lives of calves reared in crates were insufficient.
The activists complained it would take too long to phase out the use of crates, due to finish by the end of 1996, and measures to improve diets and growing space were inadequate.
The crate method is widely used by French, Italian and Dutch farmers who rear around six million calves annually to produce white meat mainly for French, Italian and German consumers.

"Group housing is not good enough and crucial animal welfare problems have not been solved. It's too soon to cry victory," Michel Vandenbosch of Global Action for the Interest of Animals (GAIA) told Reuters.
Animal rights groups have waged a long and sometimes violent campaign against confining calves in crates, which are so narrow that the animals are unable to turn around or lie down.
Vandenbosch said that calves would remain anaemic because their new diet containing hay and other fibres lacked enough iron.
The French were against increasing the level of iron because it would darken the colour of the white meat sought by consumers, said Sonja Van Tichelen of the Eurogroup for Animal Welfare.
Although the Eurogroup also wanted an earlier ban and better dietary and space conditions, it welcomed the EU decision.
"It's a good step forward. One of the major problems of intensive farming has been dealt with," she added.
The surprise agreement was struck late on Tuesday after Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates put forward a compromise which won over France, the EU's main user of veal crates.

"This was a very important breakthrough on a contentious dossier where there were clearly great differences between producers and consumers," said Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates, whose country held the EU presidency for the past six months.

France obtained a pledge that the European Commission would examine any trade distortion caused by a new early marketing subsidy scheme for calves which angry French farmers said favoured their Dutch competitors.
In the end only Italy voted against and Spain abstained.
Britain, Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Austria and Finland, who pressed for a veal crate ban, succeeded in reducing the phasing out period by two years from the original 2008 deadline.
